newsitem.title: POLAND: GDANSK SHIPYARD WORKERS SCALE DOWN PROTEST.
newsitem.headline: GDANSK SHIPYARD WORKERS SCALE DOWN PROTEST.

text.p: Workers of the failed Gdansk shipyard took to the streets on Friday for the third day running, burning tyres and shouting anti-government slogans, but their protest to save jobs appeared to subside.

Nearly 1,500 protesters gathered outside the provincial governor's office in the Baltic port city, throwing jars of red paint at the building. The city centre was filled with black, choking smoke from tyres they set on fire.
Workers blamed the government dominated by ex-communists for failing to rescue the shipyard -- cradle of the Solidarity trade union which led the overthrow of the old regime in 1989.

"The ex-communists, who are now in power destroyed the shipyard, because Solidarity was created there and because it is the mainstay of the Solidarity electoral bloc before the coming elections," Jerzy Borowczak, head of the union at the yard, told Reuters.

Solidarity leads a bloc of more than 30 small right-wing parties who are challenging the four-year-old rule of ex-communist Democratic Left Alliance (SLD) and the Peasant Party (PSL) in polls scheduled around September this year.

Friday's protest, which blocked one of Gdansk's main raod for about an hour, was smaller than those earlier this week, when the city's car, tramway and short-distance train traffic was virtually paralysed for much of the day.
But Solidarity said the protest might erupt with fresh power on Monday, when workers plan to rally outside the local Bank Gdanski , which has refused the yard a survival loan.
Solidarity has also said that by Tuesday it will have worked out plans for a nationwide protest, likely to involve strikes in selected enterprises and marches.
The union is also planning to raise funds for the yard through sale to the public of contribution coupons.

The protests in Gdansk erupted after the shipyard's receiver said last Friday he was beginning to dismiss the last 3,800 workers of the company, which has operated under bankruptcy regulations since August last year.

The receiver had wanted to secure a $100 million loan, which would have allowed him to clinch a contract to build five vessels for a German shipowner, keeping part of the yard busy while he sought an investor to save the whole business.
But despite the government offer to provide a partial guarantee for the laon, no bank agreed to extend it.

Finance Minister Marek Belka said on Friday that part of the shipyard's assets were now likely to be sold off to an investor who might undertake some work there, but he did not name any such purchaser.
"Selling the assets would mean launching production in part of the shipyard and creating jobs for some of the workers," Belka told reporters. -- Warsaw Newsroom +48 22 653 9700
